title: The Reality of Understanding
author: Becky Allen
summary: Becky Allen argues, drawing on David Deutsch's The Beginning of Infinity, that educational constructs like 'understanding,' 'fluency,' and 'misconception' are genuinely real abstractions—not because they can be directly observed, but because they are part of our best explanations for patterns of learner behavior. She opens with the central problem: identical visible performances—the same correct answer, the same well-phrased claim—can be produced by entirely different underlying capacities (retrieval, calculation, genuine understanding), and surface performance alone cannot distinguish between them. Deutsch's standard—that abstractions are real when they are part of our best explanations, like software or money—rescues educational constructs from the crude objection that they are unreal because invisible, while simultaneously raising the standard for using them. The criterion becomes explanatory necessity: 'Do I need something like understanding to explain what this learner can and cannot do, including under varied conditions?' Assessment on this account is not direct inspection of learning but the design of evidence from which we infer something about the learner's invisible capacity—making the shadows of different constructs diverge so they can be distinguished. Allen's key insight is that the problem with educational measurement is not that learning is invisible but that many different invisible things can cast the same visible shadow.
points: The same answer—'Macbeth is destroyed by ambition,' '7 × 8 = 56'—can be produced by entirely different underlying capacities; visible performance alone cannot distinguish retrieval from calculation from genuine understanding, so assessment must be designed to make these shadows diverge.

Educational abstractions like 'understanding' are real in Deutsch's sense: they are real when they are part of our best explanations for what a learner can and cannot do across varied conditions—not because they are directly observable, but because they have explanatory power.

Fluency is not one thing: the claim 'this learner is fluent' is too thin unless it specifies the range of performance it explains—fluent at what, under what conditions, across what text complexity, with what recovery capacity for the unfamiliar.

Misconceptions are explanations for patterns of wrong answers, not merely wrong answers: their usefulness lies in predicting where performance will hold and where it will break—the invisible construct earns its place by having predictive as well as retrospective explanatory power.

The problem with educational measurement is not that learning is invisible but that many different invisible things can cast the same visible shadow; good assessment is the attempt to design conditions under which those shadows diverge enough to be distinguished.
quotes: Education is full of claims about things we cannot directly see. We say that a child understands fractions. We say that another has a misconception about the equals sign. We say that a class is fluent with multiplication facts, or that they cannot transfer what they have learned to a new context.

The performance is visible. The underlying capacity may not be. Gilbert Ryle made a similar distinction between reciting multiplication facts and calculating them: the same answer can conceal different capacities.

Deutsch's point, as I understand it, is not that every abstraction we invent is real. Many abstractions are confused, dispensable or false. His point is that abstractions are real when they are part of our best explanations. They do not float outside the physical world. They matter because, when instantiated in physical systems, they help explain and change what happens.

The fact that understanding is not directly visible does not make it unreal. The fact that a misconception cannot be pointed to like a chair does not make it fictional. The question is whether these abstractions help explain patterns of learner behaviour better than the alternatives.

Assessment is not direct inspection of learning. It is the design of evidence from which we infer something about learning. Fluency, understanding and transfer are not simply names for test-score bands. They are explanatory hypotheses about the learner.

The problem with educational measurement is not that learning is invisible. It is that many different invisible things can cast the same visible shadow. Good assessment is the attempt to make those shadows diverge.
